lawyer:
Abdur Rezzaque Khan, Advocate—For the Petitioners. 
Ramzan Ali Sikdar, Advocate—For the Respondent Nos. 2 & 3.
parties:
Yusuf Ali and others ------ Petitioners
vs
Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka and others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
4. The Mirpur Mazar Co-operative Market Society Limited is an organization registered under the Co-operatives Societies Ordinance, to carry out, amongst others, the objects which are set out in its Bye-Laws. The Bye-Laws of the Society regulate the rights and obligations of its members. Article 6 of the Bye-Laws deals with the eligibility of members of the Society and Article 7 thereof deals with the procedure for selection of members of the Society. Chapter IX of the Ordinance sets out, inter alia, the provisions for settlement of disputes touching the business and affairs of a Co-operative Society. From the provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the Ordinance, it is clear that only those persons referred to in section 86 may make references for settlement of disputes under section 87. It is further evidence that the Registrar may transfer any dispute to a third person only if such person has been appointed by the Government and if the Registrar refers the dispute for disposal to one or more arbitrators, such arbitrator/arbitrators must be appointed by the Registrar himself. In the instant case, the respondent No. 5 arbitrator was not appointed by the Registrar as required under section 87(1)(c) of the Ordinance and as such the award passed by the respondent No. 5 is without lawful authority and of no legal effect. Be that as it may, the petitioners are not eligible for membership of the Society since they are merely tenants and have possessory interest in the land. Moreover, they never applied to the respondent Nos.2 and 3 and as such failure to address their applications does not arise at all. With a view to obtaining the membership of the Society, the petitioners purportedly initiated Dispute Case No. 24 of 1996 on 21-10-1996 under section 86 of the Ordinance before the District Cooperative Officer, Dhaka (respondent No. 4) who appointed the respondent No. 5 as the arbitrator to adjudicate upon the dispute. The petitioners are neither members nor are they eligible to apply for membership in terms of the Bye-Laws of the society nor do they belong to the class of per-sons authorized to initiate proceedings under section 86 of the Ordinance. The District Co-operative Officer was neither appointed by the Government under section 86 of the Ordinance to resolve the dispute nor was he authorized thereunder to appoint an arbitrator to resolve the same. Consequently, the award dated 31-3-1997 passed by the respondent No. 5 is without jurisdiction. The appellate authority (respondent No. 4) too, on a misconception of law and facts, affirmed the award passed by the respondent No. 5 However, the respondent No. 1, on a proper appreciation of the relevant laws and Bye-Laws of the Society, considered the matter in proper perspective and made the impugned decision on 29-4-2001 thereby reversing the order passed in Dispute Appeal No. 3 of 1997 upholding the award of the arbitrator made in dispute Case No. 24 of 1996. The writ petition involves highly disputed questions of facts and those cannot be resolved by reference to documents only. Besides, the writ petition is not maintainable on the ground of non-joinder of the Society as one of the respondents. So the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs. HC-54 

 10. Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan further submits that the instant writ petition is maintainable without impleading the Co-operative Society as required by section 14 in view of the fact that the management of the Society has been entrusted to its Managing Committee as provided by section 18 of the Ordinance and by that reason, the non-joinder of the Society as a respondent in the writ petition is not fatal and what is more, the respondent No. 2—President and the respondent No. 3—Secretary of the Society are already on record and such being the state of affairs, it cannot be said by any stretch of imagination that the writ petition is incompetent. 

 16. Mr Ramzan Ali Sikdar also submits that as per section 14 of the Ordinance, the Society is a necessary party; but the same has not been impleaded as a respondent in the writ petition and for non-impleading of the Society as a respondent therein, it must fail. In this connection, he has relied on the decisions in the case of Md Abdul Naim vs Chairman, Board of Directors, Sonali Bank, reported in 3 BLC (AD) 1 and in the case of Sadekullah vs Bangladesh, reported in 3 BLC 90. 

 So unless and until the petitioners have some interest in the land comprising the site of the market, they cannot become the members of the Society. Mere possessory interest in the shops will be of no avail to them in the matter of their membership of the Society of course, according to Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan, the petitioners contributed substantially to the construction and expansion of the market. Even if it is true, that does not entitle them per se to have interest in the land comprising the site of the market. What we are driving at boils down to this the subsistence of proprietary interest of the petitioners in the land comprising the site of the market in a sine qua non for becoming the members of the Society Article 6 of the Bye-Laws also provides, amongst others, that every person admitted to membership shall hold at least one share. So it appears that in order to have some interest in the land, each petitioner must hold at least one share of the Society. Moreover, his application for membership, if any, shall be supported by at least two members as postulated by Article 7(1) of the Bye-Laws. We, therefore, find substance in the submission of Mr Ramzan Ali Sikdar that any person who does not fulfil the requirement of memb6ship of the Co-operative Society shall not be eligible to be a member or to continue as a member of the Society as envisaged by Rule 3(1) of the Co-operative Societies Rules of 1987. 

 23. From the above provisions, it transpires that subject to the Co-operative Rules of 1987, the Government may by a general or special order confer all or any of the powers or impose all or any of the duties, entrusted to the Registrar by or under this Ordinance, upon any person appointed under section 6 to assist the Registrar. It is the definite assertion of Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan that the District Co-operative Officer is an Assistant Registrar and that has been mentioned by some functionaries of the Government in paragraph 13 of the Written Objection filed in Other Class Suit No. 5 of 1997. As we see it, this cannot be relied upon in the face of the denial by the respondent Nos.2 and 3. Besides, Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan has failed to point out any general or special order with regard to conferment of the powers of the Registrar upon any person appointed under section 6 to assist him from the record. In the absence of any such general or special order in that behalf, we cannot term the District Co-operative Officer (respondent No. 4) as an Assistant Registrar, or for that matter, a person appointed under section 6 to assist the Registrar. The non-conferment of powers of the Registrar upon the respondent No. 4, as is apparent from the materials on record, cuts at the very root of the case of the petitioners. So our definite conclusion is that the District Co-operative. Officer (respondent No. 4) cannot be designated as an Assistant Registrar or a person appointed under section 6 to assist the Registrar. 

 26. It is the submission of Mr Ramzan Ali Sikdar that for non-imp leading of the Society, the writ petition must fail. But according to Mr Abdur Rezzaque Khan, the writ petition will not fail because the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 being the President and the Secretary respectively of the Managing Committee of the Society are already on record. In the decision in the case of Md Abdul Naim vs Chairman, Board of Directors, Sonali Bank, reported in 3 BLC. (AD) 1 referred to by Mr Ramzan Ali Sikdar, it has been held that as the objection for not impleading the Sonali Bank, the employer of the appellant, as party was taken at the first available opportunity by the respondents and not by the Appellate Tribunal itself and such objection was re-agitated before the Appellate Tribunal who found that the application was not maintainable for which the appellant's submission that the plea of defect of party was taken after 6(six) years at the appellate stage does not hold good.
